name: Board-Level QC Questions
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Ten Minutes Before the Vote: What a Board Actually Needs to Ask
lesson.summary: A corporate board weighing a quantum computing decision needs a short, specific list of questions grounded in fiduciary duty, a predefined exit plan, and the same red flag literacy used to evaluate a pitch deck, asked out loud, in the room, before the vote.
lesson.body:
A board meeting is where fiduciary responsibility stops being a legal abstraction and becomes a specific set of questions asked out loud, on the record, before a vote. Everything the earlier chapters built, reading a pitch deck closely, deciding in advance when to walk away, weighing probability against impact, has to compress into something a board member can actually use in a room, usually with limited time and a proposal that has already generated momentum before anyone with a vote saw the details.

Picture a concrete scenario. A company's Chief Technology Officer brings the board a proposal to fund an internal quantum computing research group at 30 million dollars over three years, aimed at exploring optimization applications for the company's supply chain. The deck accompanying the proposal is polished, cites a competitor's similar announcement from six months earlier, and projects a return built mostly on a slide with the word "transformative" appearing twice. A board fulfilling its fiduciary duty does not vote on the polish. It asks a specific sequence of questions, and it insists on specific answers rather than confident tone.

The first question is the one evaluating a pitch deck already trained the reader to ask of any deck: what is the actual, falsifiable technical claim being made, what would count as evidence that it is working, and has anyone outside this proposal's authors verified any of it independently. The second question turns to the ask itself, applying fiduciary responsibility directly: has anyone estimated a realistic probability of this program producing a usable business result within the proposed window, and can that estimate be defended with something more than the fact that a competitor is doing something similar, because "our rival announced a quantum initiative" is a bandwagon signal, not a probability estimate, and a board that accepts it as one has skipped the actual analysis its duty requires.

The third question is the one that has to be answered before the money moves, not after, applying the discipline from when to cut losses in advance rather than under pressure: what are the specific, predefined milestones at six months, at eighteen months, and at three years that would tell the board this program is on track, and what result at each of those checkpoints would trigger cutting the program rather than continuing it. A board that approves 30 million dollars without agreeing on this in the same meeting is setting itself up for the exact sunk cost trap described earlier, where the second and third year of funding get approved mainly because the first year already happened, not because the evidence at that point actually supports continuing.

A useful, compact version of this for any board weighing a quantum related decision runs through four questions in order: what precisely is being claimed and who outside the room can verify it, what is the honestly estimated probability of a useful result and how was that number produced, what would the company lose if this fails outright and does that loss threaten anything the board is actually responsible for protecting, and what specific, agreed in advance evidence would end the program before the sunk cost grows too large to walk away from comfortably. None of these questions require board members to become quantum physicists. They require the same discipline this whole course has been building, refusing to let a confident narrative substitute for a probability estimate someone is willing to defend on the record, applied at the one moment, before the vote, when asking it actually changes the outcome.
